claims.text: Functional decline is often caught too late.
claims.poster_quote: Functional decline is often caught too late.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Functional decline - encompassing gait impairment, reduced mobility, and fall risk - affects more than one-third of adults over 65 and contributes to approximately three million emergency visits and $50 billion in annual U.S. healthcare expenditures. Despite this burden, functional decline lacks an automated early warning system embedded in routine clinical workflows. It is typically recognized only after observable impairment or a fall event, when the pre-clinical prevention window has closed.
claims.reason: Section: Introduction. The paper explicitly states that functional decline is often recognized too late, after observable impairment or falls.

claims.text: Trajectory matters more than single lab values.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory matters more than single lab values.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The central insight motivating this work is that the trajectory of a biomarker may carry more predictive information than any single value.
claims.reason: Section: Introduction. The paper directly states that trajectory matters more than single lab values.

claims.text: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5.
claims.poster_quote: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5 — existing tools miss this.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that has been stable for three years represents a fundamentally different risk than one that declined from 13.5 g/dL over the same period.
claims.reason: Section: Introduction. The paper explicitly compares the risk of declining versus stable hemoglobin levels.

claims.text: Existing tools miss the risk signaled by a hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years.
claims.poster_quote: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5 — existing tools miss this.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Yet, clinical interpretation focuses on whether individual values exceed reference thresholds, not on how they evolve longitudinally.
claims.reason: Section: Introduction. The paper states that existing tools miss the risk signaled by longitudinal changes like a declining hemoglobin trajectory.

claims.text: Goal: passive, zero-burden integration using only existing lab data.
claims.poster_quote: Goal: passive, zero-burden integration using only existing lab data.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Because the model uses only measurements already ordered in routine care, it supports passive, zero-burden EHR integration for early detection of pre-clinical functional decline.
claims.reason: Abstract. The paper explicitly states the goal of passive, zero-burden integration using existing lab data.

claims.text: Trajectory features beat static summaries with AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory features beat static summaries: AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: LightGBM models incorporating trajectories significantly outperformed static laboratory summaries (AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755; DeLong p < 0.001).
claims.reason: Abstract. The paper reports the AUROC comparison between trajectory features and static summaries.

claims.text: Trajectory features beat static summaries with AUPRC 0.380 vs. 0.304.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory features beat static summaries: AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755. AUPRC 0.380 vs. 0.304.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement and 3.4× the no-skill rate of 0.111.
claims.reason: Section: Results. The paper reports the AUPRC comparison between trajectory features and static summaries.

claims.text: Figure 2 shows 25% relative gain in precision-recall.
claims.poster_quote: Figure 2 shows 25% relative gain in precision-recall.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement and 3.4× the no-skill rate of 0.111 (Figure 2).
claims.reason: Section: Results. The paper explicitly states the 25% relative gain in precision-recall and references Figure 2.
